passage_notes: Factual check: Passage A tracks Madrian & Shea (2001): automatic enrollment introduced at a large U.S. firm in April 1998; participation about 37% under the old rule (for comparable-tenure workers) vs about 86% under the new one; largest effects among young and lower-income workers (and Black and Hispanic workers); default 3% contribution and money-market fund. 'Fewer than half' and 'close to ninety percent' are fair roundings. Passage B's escalation program matches Thaler & Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow (saving rates rose from about 3.5% to about 13.6% in roughly 40 months, so 'more than tripled' holds). No factual errors found.
minor: Save More Tomorrow was an opt-in commitment program, not a pure default; Passage B words this correctly ('agreed in advance'), but its tie to 'the default is the policy' is a little loose.

minor: 08 and 09 both rely on the same Passage B sentence ('Some workers who would have joined on their own and chosen to save more ended up saving less'), and 05 and 07 both test the inertia idea ('people tend to stay with whatever requires no action'). Some overlap, but no item's choices give away another item's answer.

R034-01.notes: Holding everything else constant isolates the rule change as the cause. B, C and D are not supported by the passage.

flags: minor: answer cue - B closely paraphrases the sentence just before 'never neutral' ('Because doing nothing is what most people do... it simply decides what happens when a person does nothing'), so the item is a lookup.
R034-02.notes: The stated cause is right there in the passage. A sounds plausible but is never claimed.

R034-03.notes: Freedom is 'used' by busy people. A and B tempt readers who think of physical exercise, but they make no sense with 'freedom'.

flags: minor: the stem calls it 'the finding about contribution rates', but the 'less loudly' clause is literally about the broader finding that defaults keep people in place (rates and investments). Acceptable, but it could say 'the finding that defaults keep people in place'.
R034-04.notes: 'Less loudly' means it got less attention than the undisputed participation finding. The wrong choices are weak.

flags: minor: answer cue - A paraphrases 'That same tendency' and 'not a flaw in the idea so much as the idea itself' fairly directly.
R034-05.notes: The paragraph ties the drawback to the same inertia that makes defaults work. D contradicts 'No one disputes'.

R034-06.notes: Taking the increases from future raises means take-home pay never drops. This is an unstated but standard inference. B is the trap (it twists 'few later bothered to stop them', which implies they could stop).

R034-07.notes: A says doing nothing is what most people do; B says people stay with whatever requires no action. A is the trap: B says some workers saved less, and Passage A never claims that most workers save more overall.

R034-08.notes: B's point is that participation is not the same as saving more, which complicates A's implied link between higher enrollment and more saving. A and B are facts that Passage B accepts ('No one disputes'). C is a plausible trap because Passage B says defaults are hard to escape, but that point is about inertia, not contribution rates.

flags: minor: answer cue - C paraphrases Passage B's sentence 'Some workers who would have joined on their own and chosen to save more ended up saving less' almost word for word. The cross-passage framing adds only a little difficulty.
R034-09.notes: Workers who would have joined anyway at a higher rate were held at the low default. B and D are traps built on the groups Passage A names as helped most.
